issues.legal_issue: Employees who voluntarily leave allotted housing for better concessional government accommodation are not entitled to purchase the vacated housing under a later allotment scheme when they are no longer in possession.
material_facts: The employees had initially occupied houses allotted under a rental scheme.
They voluntarily vacated those houses after receiving better government accommodation at concessional rates.
When the government adopted the relevant allotment resolution, they were not in possession of the houses, or some were in illegal occupation.
The High Court excluded this group from allotment under the hire-purchase scheme, and the exclusion was challenged on appeal.
issues.conclusion: The employees were not entitled to allotment under the hire-purchase scheme, and their exclusion was just and reasonable.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the scheme's allotment criteria to the employees' circumstances and found no error of law in the exclusion. It did not rely on an earlier case for this issue.

predicates.appeal_challenging_public_housing_allotm: The employees appealed a decision excluding them from allotment under a public housing purchase scheme.
predicates.employees_voluntarily_vacated_assigned_h: The employees voluntarily left housing previously assigned to them.
predicates.employees_received_better_concessional_h: The employees received better government housing on concessional terms after leaving the assigned housing.
predicates.employees_in_possession_at_relevant_allo: The employees were in possession of the originally assigned housing when the relevant allotment decision was made.

issues.definition: When employees appeal their exclusion after voluntarily leaving assigned housing for better concessional government housing and are no longer in possession at the relevant decision, the exclusion from the purchase allotment is valid.

issues.legal_issue: Employees permanently transferred away from the locality of their originally allotted housing are not entitled to purchase it under the hire-purchase scheme merely because they retain or occupy the housing.
material_facts: The employees had been transferred permanently from the capital to districts outside it.
Their eligibility for allotment was questioned in the proceedings.

The High Court treated them on a parity with employees who had moved away from their originally allotted houses, and the Supreme Court agreed that even employees who remained in possession could not claim allotment on that basis.
issues.conclusion: The permanently transferred employees were not entitled to allotment under the hire-purchase scheme, and their exclusion was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the same reasoning used for employees who had left their originally allotted housing: relocation away from the locality did not establish entitlement to allotment, even if an employee remained in possession. The Court did not decide the separate question about the relationship between Sections 74 and 82 of the Gujarat Housing Board Act, 1961.

predicates.appeal_challenging_public_housing_allotm: The employees appealed a decision excluding them from allotment under a public housing purchase scheme.
predicates.employees_permanently_transferred_away_f: The employees were permanently transferred away from the locality where their housing had been assigned.
predicates.employees_originally_assigned_housing_in: The employees had originally been assigned housing in the locality from which they were transferred.

issues.definition: When employees appeal their exclusion after being permanently transferred away from the locality of their originally assigned housing, the exclusion from the purchase allotment is valid.

issues.legal_issue: A cutoff for eligibility in a public housing allotment scheme is not arbitrary when it corresponds rationally to the government decision that converted the scheme to a purchase basis.
material_facts: The government decided to convert all the houses in the scheme from rental allotment to hire-purchase allotment.
The High Court used the date of that decision as the cutoff for determining eligibility for priority allotment.
The Supreme Court found that the cutoff bore a rational relationship to the purpose of allotting the houses under the converted scheme.
issues.conclusion: The cutoff was rationally connected to the allotment objective and did not violate Article 14 of the Constitution.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 does not make a cutoff arbitrary merely because another date could have been chosen; the selected date must have a rational connection to the objective. The Court found that the date of the decision to convert the scheme had that connection. No earlier case was relied on for this issue.

predicates.appeal_challenging_public_housing_eligib: The parties appealed a decision applying a cutoff to determine eligibility for public housing allotment.
predicates.government_decided_to_convert_scheme_to_: The government decided to change a housing scheme from rental allotment to purchase-based allotment.
predicates.cutoff_matches_conversion_decision: The eligibility cutoff corresponded to the government's decision to make that change.
predicates.cutoff_has_rational_connection_to_allotm: The selected cutoff bore a rational relationship to the objective of allotting housing under the converted scheme.

issues.definition: When a challenged eligibility cutoff corresponds to the decision converting a housing scheme to purchase-based allotment and rationally serves the allotment objective, the cutoff is not arbitrary.

issues.legal_issue: The constitutional right to life encompasses a right to reasonable shelter, and the State should provide permanent housing to poor people through its housing schemes within its economic means.
material_facts: The case concerned a housing scheme initially created for people in the lower-income group and weaker sections.
The Court considered constitutional protections for residence and life, as well as the State's duties concerning social and economic justice and the welfare of weaker sections.
The Court also considered the international recognition of the right to adequate housing.
issues.conclusion: The right to residence and settlement is protected by Article 19(1)(e) and is a facet of the right to life under Article 21; the State should provide permanent housing through its schemes within its economic means.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on Articles 19(1)(e), 21, 37, 38, 39(b), and 46 of the Constitution, its Preamble, and Article 11(1) of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. It applied Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation, (1985) 3 SCC 545, on the breadth of Article 21 and its protection of livelihood, and Shantistar Builders v. Narayan Khimalal Totame, AIR 1990 SC 630, on the inclusion of reasonable accommodation within the right to life.

predicates.public_housing_right_case: The proceeding concerns the constitutional right to housing in connection with a public housing scheme.
predicates.housing_scheme_targets_weaker_sections: The housing scheme was created to benefit poorer or otherwise weaker sections of society.
predicates.constitutional_right_to_residence_is_inv: The parties invoke constitutional protection for residence and life in relation to access to housing.

issues.definition: When a constitutional housing-right proceeding concerns a scheme for weaker sections and invokes the right to residence, the right to life includes reasonable shelter and the State should facilitate housing within its means.
